guards.rule: A scene check failure on a level means the build stage produced geometry that violates the level's constraints; rerunning the build stage regenerates the level geometry and re-validates it.

A washbasin that is placed awkwardly on a small shelf next to the tub, not in a proper vanity unit, should be swapped for a model that includes a vanity unit or is designed to be wall-hung at the correct height.
A tall dresser placed in the middle of a room, acting as a bulky partition, should be swapped for a lower or slimmer model that does not block the flow of space.
A piece that is planned to be built but has no object in the scene should be retyped to its correct type to force a rebuild with a suitable model.
A window that is not seen in a view that must show it should be addressed by adjusting the camera to include the window in the frame.

Drawing strokes on the furniture layer that are not used by any piece should be checked for whether they represent furniture that was lost during the reading stage. If they do, the reading stage should be improved to recognize them.
A room that has a second label in the documents but is not a room of its own in the model should be split into two rooms during the reading stage.
A piece that is named in the documents but has no corresponding piece in the model should be added to the model during the reading stage.
A piece that was removed by AI but is a valid piece in the room should be retyped to its correct type to force a rebuild with a suitable model.
A cluster of drawn pieces that is too large to be a single furniture piece and does not fit any type should be marked as not furniture with the evidence from the plan crop.
A piece that was not built because it cut another piece and no free place was found within 1.0 m should be moved to the nearest free place in the room.
A piece removed by the AI that is a valid type for its room (a shoe cabinet in a hall) must be rebuilt by retyping it to its own type, not to a different type that fits its footprint.
A piece removed by the AI that is a valid type for its room (a desk in a bedroom) must be rebuilt by retyping it to its own type.

A piece that blocks a walkway must be moved to a free place that clears the walkway, not removed.
A decor item that depends on a piece which was not built must be resolved by rebuilding the host piece.
Site areas labeled in the documents (e.g., VERANDA, BALKON) must be built with an outline and structure if they are primary outdoor living spaces.

A kitchen must have its main functional anchor (stove/hob) visible and at working height on the counter.
A room's main functional pieces (desk, office chair, armchairs, floor lamp) must be visible in the render.

A bathroom's washbasin must be visible in the render and not a crude placeholder.
A room's main functional pieces (desk, office chair, armchairs) must be visible in the render.
A wardrobe must be visible in the render and not block a door or window.
A dresser must be visible in the render.
A dressing room must have a dressing area (e.g., a bench, a mirror, a rail) visible in the render.

A drawn bathroom fixture that overlaps a partner fixture and has no free place within its move limits is a fit failure: the solver must re-solve the bathroom set as one unit around the drawn anchor rather than leaving the overlap open for the architect.
A piece that blocks the sightline or passage through a window opening must be moved or removed; the fit stage must check that no furniture stands in the clear zone of any opening.
A kitchen counter built with its top above working height (0.97 m) is a fitting error: the parametric mesh was chosen without checking the vertical placement against the working-height rule.

An entrance with both a ramp and stairs competing for the same space is a build error: the entrance solution must be a single, coherent choice (steps, ramp, or none) that matches the site grade difference.
A room typed as 'other' with only a wardrobe is not a functional room type; it should be typed as 'storage' (or 'dressing' if the program supports it) to match its contents and area.

When a document names a piece (e.g., a dresser) at a specific location and the nearest valid placement is more than 1 m away, the fit stage must either (a) relax the placement constraint to allow the piece at the named location if it does not clash, or (b) flag the discrepancy for the architect rather than silently dropping the piece.

An opening in the outer wall that is fully or mostly blocked by furniture and has no passage function should be read as a window, not a door. The reading stage must check whether the opening is a passage or a window based on its clear width and the furniture in its approach.

An outer-wall opening whose approach is blocked by drawn furniture and that has no swing arc is a window, not a door; the reading must classify it by its sill and the furniture in front of it, not by its width.
A movable sanitary piece (washbasin) that overlaps a fixed drawn piece (bathtub) must be repositioned to clear it; the fit stage must resolve the clash by moving the movable piece, not the fixed one.
A furniture piece that covers a window blocks light and ventilation and must be moved to clear the opening; the fit stage must keep furniture off window sills.
The big loop must run enough cycles to raise the house score; a single cycle that hits the deadline without improving the score is a process failure that requires more cycles.
Views marked for review by the check stage must be addressed by the agent in the next round; the agent must re-frame or remove cameras that fail the review.

When the agent's swap_model attempts for a washbasin are all refused by fit rules (caps, height), the code must allow at least one model from the piece's allowed list that passes the fit rules, or the agent must be given a different tool (e.g. resize_piece) to adjust the piece to fit a better model.

When the agent's swap_model attempts for a washbasin are all refused by fit rules (caps, height, sloped ceiling), the code must allow at least one model from the piece's allowed list that passes the fit rules, or the agent must be given a different tool (e.g. resize_piece) to adjust the piece to fit a better model.

A drawn floor lamp that blocks the free zone in front of a drawn armchair must be repositioned by the fit stage; the drawn_lock constraint (0.3 m max move) must not prevent resolving a physical clash between two drawn pieces.

When the agent's relayout_room attempts for a large living room are refused because they do not resolve a walkway constraint (G11), the code must allow the relayout to proceed if the walkway constraint is satisfied by the new layout, or the agent must be given a tool to adjust the door positions.

When a drawn wardrobe is not built because its cluster is larger than 4.5 m on a side, the code must either build the wardrobe as a separate piece or allow the cluster to be split; the 'not built' reason must not hide a loss of a drawn element.
A camera in a small room (dressing room) must be positioned to show the room's main function and furniture, not pressed against a wall framing only a door and a sliver of a wardrobe.
Outdoor furniture on a terrace or balcony must be a coherent set (matching style, material, and design concept), not a random assortment of mismatched pieces.
Interior renders must include the room's lighting and material styling layers; a bare grey-box render of a furnished room is a failure of the render stage, not the model.
Bathroom renders must include warm ambient lighting and styled surfaces to match the project's reference aesthetic; a sterile white box is unacceptable.
Interior camera views must frame all key fixtures of the room without cutting them off at the frame edges.
Kitchen renders must convey a warm, lived-in feel with styled surfaces, plants, and warm lighting; a sterile box with mismatched furniture is a render and styling failure.
Kitchen rooms must include decorative elements (plants, wall art, counter decor) and warm lighting to create a cozy atmosphere; a bare kitchen is a styling failure.
Dining chairs must match the style and color of the dining table and the room's overall aesthetic; a single mismatched chair is a fit failure.
Kitchen renders must convey a warm, textured, lived-in feel; a sterile box with boxy mismatched furniture is a render and styling failure.
Kitchen appliances must match the style and finish of the cabinetry and the room's overall aesthetic; a glossy black fridge in a matte rustic-white kitchen is a fit failure.
Dining tables must match the style and color of the room's overall aesthetic; a round wooden table in a stark minimalist white kitchen is a fit failure.
Kitchen renders must convey a warm, textured, lived-in feel with coherent furniture; a grey box with sparse blocky furniture is a render and styling failure.
Living rooms must include wall art or mirrors to anchor the space; large empty walls are a styling failure.
Dining tables must include decorative elements (centerpiece, runner, bowl of fruit) to look styled; a bare table is a styling failure.
Living room sofas must form a cohesive palette and style; a rust-colored leather sofa clashing with a white sofa and red egg chair is a fit failure.
Living room renders must convey a mid-century aesthetic with cohesive furniture and styling layers; a flat beige box with mismatched furniture is a render and styling failure.
Living room sofas must form a cohesive palette and style; a plain beige sofa clashing with a rust-orange sofa is a fit failure.
Living room seating areas must include wall art or mirrors to anchor the space; a large blank wall is a styling failure.
Interior renders of wet rooms must include warm accent lighting and styled surfaces (textiles, wood, accessories) to avoid a sterile, unfinished appearance.
Bathroom scenes must include at least one warm light source (e.g., pendant, sconce) to create a cozy atmosphere, not just flat daylight.

When a fixture is under a sloped ceiling and all standard library models are refused for height, the fitting stage should prioritize low-profile or wall-hung models that fit the clearance, or flag the geometry for review rather than leaving a crude placeholder.
Camera views of bathrooms must frame the main functional group (vanity, toilet, shower) and include styling elements to avoid a 'grey box' appearance.
Furniture in a children's room must be stylistically coherent and finished; raw slabs and mismatched office chairs are not acceptable.
Wardrobe models must have visible doors, handles, and depth to read as functional furniture, not flat slabs.
Desk models must have finished surfaces and legs that match the room's style (e.g., light wood for Scandinavian).
Office chairs in bedrooms/children's rooms should be light-colored and stylistically appropriate, not dark glossy plastic.
Children's room renders must show a coherent, stylish furniture set, not a mismatched office corner.
Furniture in a single room must be from a coherent design family to avoid a chaotic, mismatched appearance.
When a room has multiple beds, they must be from the same design family or style to appear as a matching set.
Bathroom camera views must frame the main functional group (shower, toilet, washbasin) to show the room's layout and styling.
Camera views must include the main fixtures of the room to avoid a 'bare corner' appearance.
Bathroom scenes must include styled surfaces and accessories to avoid a bare, empty appearance.
Bedroom renders must show the full furniture set and styling layers to avoid a bare, unfinished appearance.
Bedroom scenes must include layered, cozy styling (throws, cushions, rugs) to avoid a flat, bare appearance.

When a bedroom wall carries two full-height door openings side by side, the reading must not build both as doors: it must check the plan for a window, a built-in closet opening, or a wall line and resolve the second opening accordingly before the model stage.
The exterior site must carry the reference's planting and hardscape (hedges, trees, a path to the entrance) so the facade is not a bare white box.
The entrance must read as a designed threshold: a path and a front court (and seating where the reference shows it) rather than a bare slab door.

A decor cushion that penetrates its host by more than 0.03 m must be re-seated on the host's top surface (or dropped) rather than left unbuilt; the rest check should nudge the cushion up to the host's seat plane instead of refusing it.
A desk in a bedroom must be placed near the window for natural light and within reach of the bed, not in the middle of a wall creating a dead zone.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece and must not be built as a separate piece, even if an AI pass names it a type that fits its size; the reading stage should suppress it as a detail.
The reading stage must read ATTDEF entities (attribute definitions) in DWG files; 28 ATTDEF entities were not read, which may hold room labels, dimensions or other data the ledger checks.

Site decor read outside the walls of L1 (the upper floor) must be mapped to L0 (the ground floor, where the site is) and used in the site build; 35 decor items were read but not used, 20 of them repeating the ground plan's symbols at the same place.

When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. 'Salon' and 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ'), the reading stage must split the room into two (living and dining) rather than keeping one room with a second label; the split should use the second label's anchor and area.
Every printed area label on a plan must be bound to the room outline it sits in and stored on that room's record; an unbound area label is a lost check, not a warning.
When the reading selects a wall layer by evidence and documents the primitives it excluded, that is a correct, auditable decision, not a lost element.
Decor symbols read on an upper floor that duplicate the ground floor's site symbols at the same coordinates are a known artifact (site.decor_other_levels) and are correctly excluded from the model.

Any layer whose name indicates a building element (e.g. DENIZLIK = bathtub/basin, DUVAR = wall, PENCERE = window) must be either used by the model or explicitly named in a warning with the reason it was excluded; a silent, unused named layer is a loss.
A piece placed by the decor stage and dropped by the agent stage is a loss; the agent's next round must restore or re-place it.
A dining table in a living/dining room should have at least a tablecloth or a simple setting; a bare table is an incomplete decor.
Armchairs in a bedroom should match the room's palette and style; a mismatched set (e.g. modern plastic in a warm, neutral room) is a decor error.
A piece listed in a room's data must be placed and visible in the render; a listed-but-invisible piece is a loss.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms, the reading must either split the outline into two rooms or assign the extra label to a separate room; a single outline with two labels is a misread.
A kitchen counter must be built with visible appliances and a proper layout; a bare box without appliances is a placeholder, not a kitchen.
A desk and chair in a children's room should be sized and styled for a child; a large, formal office setup is a mismatch.
A chair that differs from its drawn place by more than the tolerance (0.05 m) must be swapped for a model that fits its drawn position.
A dresser that differs from its drawn place by more than the tolerance (0.05 m) must be swapped for a model that fits its drawn position.
A small (<= 4 m2) hall/entry room that holds a shoe cabinet is a plausible entrance storage nook; the type 'hall' is correct and no change is needed.
A hall containing a shoe cabinet and a stair is a plausible entrance hall; no change is needed.
A bathroom containing a shower, toilet and washbasin is a plausible bathroom; no change is needed.
A bathroom containing a bathtub, toilet, washbasin and washing machine is a plausible bathroom; no change is needed.
A bedroom containing a single bed, dresser, nightstand and wardrobe is a plausible bedroom; no change is needed.
A bedroom containing a double bed, desk, dresser, nightstand, office chair and wardrobe is a plausible bedroom; no change is needed.
A bedroom containing an armchair, double bed, desk, floor lamp, nightstand and office chair is a plausible bedroom; no change is needed.
A living room containing an armchair, bookshelf, chair, floor lamp, potted plant, sofa, coffee table and dining table is a plausible living room; no change is needed.
A kitchen containing a chair, fridge, counter, sink, stair, stove, dining table and wall cabinet is a plausible kitchen; no change is needed.
A small hall with no pieces is a plausible hall; no change is needed.
A bathroom containing a bathtub, toilet and washbasin is a plausible bathroom; no change is needed.
A fitter must not place a piece so that the ray from an opening hits it (the piece covers the window's clear zone); the piece must be moved clear of the opening's clear zone.

When an elevation's openings are to be checked against the plans, the reading must record the elevation's side (from the north arrow or a labelled side); if no side can be determined, the check is skipped and the elevation is flagged as 'side unknown' rather than silently left unchecked.

When a drawn section is to be checked point-by-point against the roof, the reading must verify that the section line runs one-to-one with the plan (its ends within 0.30 m of the roof outline's ends along the section axis); if not, the check is skipped and the section is flagged as 'not aligned with plan' rather than silently left unchecked.
guards.target: the drawn section r# is not checked point by point against the roof

guards.rule: When an elevation is to be compared with the model, the reading must record the elevation's view bearing or side; if neither can be determined, the comparison is skipped and the elevation is flagged as 'bearing unknown' rather than silently left uncomparable.

When a drawn dining group's anchor (table) is locked by the drawing and the solver finds no free span that fits the full group, it must stop after the first failed span and report the group as 'drawn-locked, no free span' instead of retrying the same locked anchor on other spans until max_tries; the drawn anchor is the cause, not the span.

The fitting stage must not fall back to a parametric mesh for a wall_cabinet when a library model of the correct type and size exists; it must search the library for a wall_cabinet model that fits the drawn footprint before using parametric.

The fitting stage must not refuse a generated model when it is the only model of the correct type that fits the drawn footprint; it must accept the generated model and flag it for review rather than leaving the piece with a placeholder-looking model.

When the reading records the same opening twice (same span, same width), the build stage merges them into one element and the conservation check must treat the duplicate record as resolved, not as a loss.
Axis bubbles, level marks, and other drawing annotations on layers like 'AKS YAZI' or 'AKS' are never built; the conservation check should not flag them as lost elements.
Small drawn shapes (under 0.30 m) that lie entirely inside a larger piece's footprint are treated as cushions or details of that piece, not as independent furniture to be built.
When a library model for a piece includes built-in cushions or pillows, separately drawn cushion elements on that piece are not built as independent objects.
Decor or detail elements that depend on a host piece are only built if the host piece is built; if the host is not built, the decor is correctly omitted.
Axis bubbles on layers like 'AKS' are drawing annotations and are never built.
Structural columns that support a veranda or balcony are built as part of that structure's posts, not as separate column elements.
Level marks on layers like 'kot' are drawing annotations and are never built as physical elements.
Site area labels (veranda, balcony) are represented by the ground/paving surfaces in the site model, not as separate built elements.
When two drawn outlines represent the same physical object (one inside the other, same type), the build stage merges them into one element.
A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece of the same type is treated as a duplicate or part of the larger piece, not as an independent element.

When a kitchen run is drawn as a single outline containing its fixtures (sink, stove, etc.), the build stage decomposes it into individual counter segments and fixtures rather than building the outline as one piece.
A drawn outline that surrounds 3 or more other pieces and is larger than any single piece is treated as a rug or zone outline, not as furniture.
Small drawn shapes (under 0.30 m) that lie entirely inside a sofa's footprint are treated as cushions or details, not as independent furniture.

When a piece is removed by an AI decision (AI.remove_piece) but the drawing clearly shows it as a distinct, correctly-typed piece in a room that allows that type, the build stage should not drop it; the removal decision should be reviewed.
A conservation finding whose 'not built' reason is 'the answer to AI.remove_piece:<id>' is a false alarm: the removal was a deliberate decision, not a stage dropping a drawn element.

An untyped drawn mark that is a long thin cluster (>4.5 m on one side, <0.7 m on the other) in a bedroom is a dimension line or outline fragment, not furniture; the build stage may refuse it without a loss.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m that fits no furniture type is a detail line (threshold, valve, shelf edge), not a buildable piece; the build stage may refuse it without a loss.
A drawn mark that is 60% or more contained within another built piece is a detail of that piece, not a separate furniture item; the build stage may refuse it without a loss.

When a nightstand is not built because it overlaps a bed and no free place is within 1.0 m, the furniture agent must re-solve the bedroom layout (relayout_room or place_group) to find a valid position for the nightstand.
A stair piece on the top floor that 'arrives from' the floor below and has 'no level above' is correctly not built again; it is the same physical stair, not a new one.
A decoration that is 'not built: its host <id> is not built' is a false alarm when the host was removed by an explicit AI decision; the decoration is correctly absent.
A decoration that is 'not built: its host <id> is not built' is a real loss when the host is a standard furniture piece that should be built; fix the host first.
null
When a furniture name text is found in a room that already contains a piece of that type, the text is considered satisfied and no new piece is added.

When a furniture name text names a piece type not present in the room, and the room's area is sufficient, the solver should place the piece at the text's location or the nearest valid spot, even if it is more than 1 m from the text, as long as it is within the room and clear of doors and other pieces.
An outer-wall opening whose approach is blocked by a drawn piece and that has no outside destination is a window, not a door.
A hall under 3 m2 is a passage and needs no furniture.
A drawn piece that overlaps a drawn fixture in a wet room is moved to the nearest free place, clear of the fixture and the window.
A drawn piece that covers a window is moved to the nearest free place, clear of the window.
A labelled outdoor site area (veranda, terrace, balcony) that is drawn in the plan must be built as a platform with its drawn outline, even if it is not a room.
A labelled outdoor area (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a platform with its own floor and railing, not dropped as 'no outline'.
A room typed as a dressing room (soyunma odası) must be furnished with its dressing set (bench, mirror, storage) so its purpose is legible; a bare wardrobe is not a dressing room.
An interior camera must frame the room's main group, not a wall or door leaf; if the only furniture is a wardrobe, the view must show it.
An interior camera must frame the room's contents (here the shoe cabinet and doors), not a bare wall corner.
A scene check failure on a level is a build-stage defect; re-run the build for that level to re-fit the offending pieces.
A dresser that floats or intersects a wall/window is a bad model fit; swap to a model whose depth clears the wall and whose front faces the room.
A planned piece that is missing from the scene is a build loss; retype it to force a rebuild with a suitable model.
An exterior view that must show a window must frame it; if the window is not in the frame, re-aim the camera at it.
Strokes on the furniture layer inside a room that no piece uses must be read as furniture (a sofa, chairs around a table) and built, not dropped.
A second label inside a room outline (e.g. 'ANTRE') is a separate room the reading must split out, not a duplicate label of the same room.
A named piece in the documents (e.g. '*SIFONIYER' = dresser) that the model lacks must be added at its named location.
A piece removed by AI that is a valid piece in its room must be rebuilt; retyping it forces a rebuild with a suitable model.

A drawn cluster wider than 4.5 m that is not a single furniture type is a built-in or architectural element (e.g. a long low bench, window seat, or storage run); the build stage must model it as a built-in module rather than dropping it as 'not furniture', and the mark_not_furniture tool must not be used for a drawn element that the documents show as a functional part of the room.
none

Site areas labeled in the documents (e.g. VERANDA, BALKON) must be built as structural outlines with floors and railings when they are primary outdoor living spaces; the site stage must not skip them as 'no outline' when the documents clearly label them.
A children's room (Çocuk Odası) whose drawn anchor is a double bed is a misread: the room's function is two sleepers, so the anchor is a bunk bed (or loft bed), not a single double bed.
A hall's anchor piece (shoe cabinet) that is 'not built' leaves the room empty in the render; the anchor must be built with a real model, not left parametric or absent.

A bathtub and a washbasin that overlap with no free place within the move limits means the bathroom set was placed without checking the wet-room clearance; the set must be re-solved as a unit so the basin clears the tub.
A window whose sightline is blocked by furniture means the furniture was placed without checking the window clearance; the piece must be moved or the window re-placed so the view through is clear.
A kitchen counter built with its top at 2.10 m over the floor is a misread size: the counter's working height is 0.90-0.97 m, so the piece must be resized to a real counter height.
A washbasin placed at the level of the bathtub rim is a misread height: the basin's rim must be at 0.85 m working height, not at tub-rim level.
A dresser that renders as a floating white railing is a wrong model: the model does not match the piece's type, so it must be swapped to a real dresser model.

An entrance with a handrail that does not connect to the steps and a floating canopy is a broken entrance: the entrance solution must be set so the steps, handrail and canopy are built as a coherent unit.
A room typed 'other' that contains only a wardrobe is a misread type: a room with a wardrobe and no other fixtures is a storage/dressing room, not 'other'.

A dresser named in the documents (TEXT) that cannot be placed because the nearest valid spot is more than 1 m from the text is a fit failure: the fit stage must place the piece at the text's location even if it is not the nearest valid spot, or the text's location must be checked against the room's walls and doors before the fit stage runs.

A 2.15 m sliding door read from its lines (no swing arc) in the outer wall of a living room, with a drawn piece standing across its approach, is a misread: it is a window at the floor's sill, not a door.
A window in a wet room with furniture placed in front of it is not a passage blockage; the furniture placement is a fit issue, not a reading error.
A window in a kitchen with a counter placed in front of it is not a passage blockage; the furniture placement is a fit issue, not a reading error.
A window in a living room with furniture placed in front of it is not a passage blockage; the furniture placement is a fit issue, not a reading error.
A window in a bedroom with furniture placed in front of it is not a passage blockage; the furniture placement is a fit issue, not a reading error.
A window in a hall with furniture placed in front of it is not a passage blockage; the furniture placement is a fit issue, not a reading error.
Furniture pieces in a bathroom must not overlap; the washbasin should be placed clear of the bathtub.
Furniture pieces must not cover windows; they should be placed clear of the window to allow light and ventilation.
The big loop should run for at least 2 cycles to allow the agent to improve the house score, unless the deadline is reached.
Views marked for review should be adjusted to show the room's key features and avoid showing bare walls or cluttered corners.
Outdoor areas should be furnished with appropriate outdoor furniture (e.g., seating, tables, plants) to match the project's style and reference.
Bathroom renders should include styled surfaces (e.g., warm wood, stone) and the washbasin should be placed at a logical height (e.g., wall-hung at 0.85 m).
Bathroom walls should be clad with natural materials (e.g., warm wood, stone) to match the project's style and reference.
A kitchen render must show a styled dining set, wall art, and warm lighting; blocky primitive models and bare walls are a failure of the styling stage, not the geometry.
Every habitable room in a styled project must have at least one wall art piece; bare walls are a missing decor layer.
A kitchen render must show a complete, styled kitchen with wall cabinets, a cohesive dining set, and warm lighting; blocky primitives and bare counters are a styling failure.
Furniture models must match the project's style (Scandinavian: wood, woven light, art, styled surfaces); blocky primitives are a model-selection failure.
A dining table model must match the project's style (Scandinavian/minimal); a simple oval slab that clashes with the light, airy style is a model-selection failure.
A living room render must show a cohesive furniture palette and decor layers (art, lighting, textiles); a chaotic mix of clashing styles is a styling failure.
An armchair model must match the project's style (Scandinavian/minimal); a loud 1960s design piece that clashes with the neutral palette is a model-selection failure.
A sofa model must match the project's style (Scandinavian/modern); an orange leather sofa that clashes with the grey sofa and other chairs is a model-selection failure.
A living room's central seating area must have a coffee table as an anchor and styled surface; an empty central area is a missing functional piece.
A living room render must show a cohesive furniture palette and decor layers; a bare, unfinished shell with mismatched models is a styling failure.
A sofa model must match the project's style (Scandinavian/modern); a dated, bulky model that clashes with the modern, light style is a model-selection failure.
A living room render must show a cohesive furniture palette; a mismatched collection of styles (rust leather, red egg chair, white sofa, glass dining) is a styling failure.
A bathroom render must show a cohesive, styled space with warm lighting and textured surfaces; a floating black washbasin and flat, cold light are a styling failure.
A washbasin model must match the project's style (minimal/scandinavian) and the room's palette (white); a floating, boxy black placeholder is a model-selection failure.
A bathroom render must show warm, inviting lighting; flat, cold, clinical light is a lighting failure.
A bedroom render must show a coherent spatial arrangement; floating, overlapping, or impossible furniture placement is a layout failure.

A bedroom sized for one sleeper (under ~25 m2 without a second drawn bed) is furnished with a single bed; a second full bed is only built when the drawing shows two beds or the room is a twin/dormitory.
Every room with a large window or balcony door gets a softening layer (curtains or blinds) in the furnishing pass; bare glazing is a missing layer, not a finished look.

An interior camera must be placed at a free point that shows the room's main pieces and is not blocked by a railing, partition or furniture edge; a view whose foreground is a structural element that hides the room is a bad camera, not a bad room.

A bed model whose mattress is a flat box and whose throw is an untextured decal is a crude placeholder; the furniture agent must pick a model with a real mattress, frame and bedding that matches the project's style.

A room typed as a children's room is furnished with age-appropriate, playful, layered pieces (bed, desk, storage, rug, plants, art) in the project's style; a generic adult bedroom set is a style mismatch, not a valid furnishing.

A bathroom camera must be placed at a free point that shows the room's main fixtures (shower, basin, toilet) and is not pressed against a wall or partition; a close-up of a corner that hides the fixtures is a bad camera.
A room whose reference style is defined by abundant greenery gets multiple plants (hanging, floor, windowsill) in the furnishing pass; a single low-poly plant is a missing layer, not a finished look.

Furniture in one room must share a cohesive style; a mid-century modern armchair that clashes with the room's rustic pine and modern grey pieces is a style mismatch that the furniture agent must resolve by swapping to a model that fits the room's set.

A nightstand and its lamp must match the room's style; a rustic pine nightstand with a harsh modern lamp that clashes with the bed and chairs is a style mismatch that the furniture agent must resolve by swapping to a model that fits the room's set.

A hall camera must be placed at a free point that shows the room's anchor pieces (shoe cabinet, mirror, art) and is not a bare stair landing; a view that reads as a construction site is a bad camera or a missing furnishing layer.

A hall/entrance room gets an anchor piece (shoe cabinet, console, mirror) and at least one styling layer (art, lighting, warm material) in the furnishing pass; a bare hall is a missing layer, not a finished look.
A hall camera must be placed at a free point that shows the room's doors and anchor pieces; a close-up of a wall corner and louvered panel that hides the hall is a bad camera.
A bedroom whose reference shows a textured rug gets a rug with real texture in the furnishing pass; a flat, untextured mat is a missing layer, not a finished look.

A bedroom must be furnished with warm, layered, organic materials (plants, textiles, art, warm light) in the project's style; a 'grey box' with a bed and flat untextured surfaces is a missing styling layer, not a finished look.

A dressing room camera must be placed at a free point that shows the room's main group (wardrobe, mirror, seating) and is not pressed against furniture; a tight close-up of a door and wardrobe edge is a bad camera.
An interior camera must frame the room's furniture, never a bare wall or door frame; if the room is too small to show its pieces, the view is removed rather than left on a wall.

Exterior presentation views must be rendered with the facade's material palette (cladding, frames, roof) and the site's landscaping and lighting applied; a grey-box massing study is not an acceptable client exterior.
The facade material slot must carry the project's cladding look (wood/stone) so the exterior is not a flat untextured box.
The site must carry landscaping (trees, hedge, planters) so the exterior is not a flat empty green plane.
A decor cushion that cannot rest on its host without penetration is correctly left unbuilt; it is a minor cosmetic item, not a lost piece.
A bed model whose bedding renders as a mess (askew pillows, crumpled throw) should be swapped for a model with cleaner bedding geometry.
A drawn piece that is 60%+ inside another piece but whose size and AI naming fit a distinct furniture type (e.g. a 0.40 m floor lamp beside a bed) is a lost piece, not a detail of the host.
The DWG reader must parse ATTDEF (attribute definition) entities in addition to TEXT and MTEXT, so that block attributes (room labels, dimensions, notes) are not silently dropped.
Site decor read on an upper level (L1) that duplicates the ground-floor (L0) symbols at the same location is a reading artefact and should be discarded, not carried into the site model.
When a room outline holds two room labels, the reading must split the outline at the wall between them so each label becomes its own room, instead of keeping the larger label and dropping the other.
Every printed area label on a plan must be bound to its room so the area check can run; an unbound label is a lost check.
A reading warning that records the evidence for a chosen wall layer and the count of primitives left out is an informational note, not a lost element.
Decor symbols read on an upper level that duplicate the ground plan's symbols at the same place are not used, because the site belongs to the ground floor.
A drawing layer whose name denotes a sanitary fixture (e.g. DENIZLIK = bidet) must be read as that fixture and placed in the matching wet room, not left unused and unnamed.
A piece placed by the decor stage must not be dropped by the agent stage; if the agent removes it, its next round must restore or re-place it.
A dining table in a furnished home should be styled (setting, cloth or props) so the surface is not bare in the render.
Furniture in a room must match the room's palette and style; a mismatched set should be swapped for a model that fits.
A piece listed in a room's data must be visible in the room's render; if it is not, the agent must place or re-place it so it shows.
A drawn piece must be built within the drawing tolerance of its drawn place; a layout offset beyond tolerance must be corrected.

Every elevation sheet must carry a north arrow or a side label; if the drawing lacks one, the reading stage must infer the side from the plan's section cut line and record it, so the elevation-to-plan opening check can run.

A section is only comparable to the plan/roof when its cut line matches the plan outline within 0.30 m at both ends and its roof line is monotonic; if not, the reading stage must flag the section as non-comparable and skip the point-by-point check instead of forcing it.

guards.rule: Every elevation must be assigned a view bearing or side at reading time (from its north arrow, side label, or the plan's section cut line); if none can be determined, the elevation is marked non-comparable and excluded from the model comparison rather than silently skipped.

A parametric opening built in the style's finish when no library model of the building's window family fits the drawn size is a correct fallback, not a defect: it keeps one door and window language and the opening is present.
When a drawn kitchen fitting is built as a parametric mesh below the library level, swap it to a library model of the same type and matching footprint so it renders at library quality.
The library must carry at least one wall_cabinet model per common kitchen footprint (e.g. 0.90 x 0.35 m) so a drawn wall cabinet is never forced to a parametric mesh below the library level.
The library must carry at least one wall_cabinet model per common kitchen footprint (e.g. 0.59 x 0.35 m) so a drawn wall cabinet is never forced to a parametric mesh below the library level.
A kitchen worktop and backsplash must carry a textured material (stone, wood or tile) rather than a flat untextured surface, so the kitchen does not read as a grey box.

A dining table model must match the room's stated style (here modern/minimal); an ornate, textured-base table is a style mismatch and should be swapped for a minimal/modern model of the same footprint.

A statement armchair must fit the room's cohesive style; a bold, dated piece (e.g. a red egg chair) in a modern/minimal room is a style mismatch and should be swapped for a minimal/modern model of the same footprint.

Large interior windows should carry a simple curtain or soft layer by default so they do not read as bare glass in renders; the scene stage should add a curtain layer to large openings unless the style is explicitly bare.
A wardrobe model must match the room's warm wood tones; a flat white generic unit is a style mismatch and should be swapped for a minimal/modern or scandinavian model of the same footprint.
A bed model must include layered bedding (duvet, throw, textured pillows) rather than a single flat sheet, so the bedroom reads as styled, not clinical.

rules_proposed.rule: A camera in a small room (dressing room) must be positioned to show the room's main function and furniture, not pressed against a wall framing only a door and a sliver of a wardrobe.
Outdoor furniture on a terrace or balcony must be a coherent set (matching style, material, and design concept), not a random assortment of mismatched pieces.
Interior renders must include the room's lighting and material styling layers; a bare grey-box render of a furnished room is a failure of the render stage, not the model.
Bathroom renders must include warm ambient lighting and styled surfaces to match the project's reference aesthetic; a sterile white box is unacceptable.
Interior camera views must frame all key fixtures of the room without cutting them off at the frame edges.
Kitchen renders must convey a warm, lived-in feel with styled surfaces, plants, and warm lighting; a sterile box with mismatched furniture is a render and styling failure.
Kitchen rooms must include decorative elements (plants, wall art, counter decor) and warm lighting to create a cozy atmosphere; a bare kitchen is a styling failure.
Dining chairs must match the style and color of the dining table and the room's overall aesthetic; a single mismatched chair is a fit failure.
Kitchen renders must convey a warm, textured, lived-in feel; a sterile box with boxy mismatched furniture is a render and styling failure.
Kitchen appliances must match the style and finish of the cabinetry and the room's overall aesthetic; a glossy black fridge in a matte rustic-white kitchen is a fit failure.
Dining tables must match the style and color of the room's overall aesthetic; a round wooden table in a stark minimalist white kitchen is a fit failure.
Kitchen renders must convey a warm, textured, lived-in feel with coherent furniture; a grey box with sparse blocky furniture is a render and styling failure.
Living rooms must include wall art or mirrors to anchor the space; large empty walls are a styling failure.
Dining tables must include decorative elements (centerpiece, runner, bowl of fruit) to look styled; a bare table is a styling failure.
Living room sofas must form a cohesive palette and style; a rust-colored leather sofa clashing with a white sofa and red egg chair is a fit failure.
Living room renders must convey a mid-century aesthetic with cohesive furniture and styling layers; a flat beige box with mismatched furniture is a render and styling failure.
Living room sofas must form a cohesive palette and style; a plain beige sofa clashing with a rust-orange sofa is a fit failure.
Living room seating areas must include wall art or mirrors to anchor the space; a large blank wall is a styling failure.
Interior renders of wet rooms must include warm accent lighting and styled surfaces (textiles, wood, accessories) to avoid a sterile, unfinished appearance.
Bathroom scenes must include at least one warm light source (e.g., pendant, sconce) to create a cozy atmosphere, not just flat daylight.

When a fixture is under a sloped ceiling and all standard library models are refused for height, the fitting stage should prioritize low-profile or wall-hung models that fit the clearance, or flag the geometry for review rather than leaving a crude placeholder.
Camera views of bathrooms must frame the main functional group (vanity, toilet, shower) and include styling elements to avoid a 'grey box' appearance.
Furniture in a children's room must be stylistically coherent and finished; raw slabs and mismatched office chairs are not acceptable.
Wardrobe models must have visible doors, handles, and depth to read as functional furniture, not flat slabs.
Desk models must have finished surfaces and legs that match the room's style (e.g., light wood for Scandinavian).
Office chairs in bedrooms/children's rooms should be light-colored and stylistically appropriate, not dark glossy plastic.
Children's room renders must show a coherent, stylish furniture set, not a mismatched office corner.
Furniture in a single room must be from a coherent design family to avoid a chaotic, mismatched appearance.
When a room has multiple beds, they must be from the same design family or style to appear as a matching set.
Bathroom camera views must frame the main functional group (shower, toilet, washbasin) to show the room's layout and styling.
Camera views must include the main fixtures of the room to avoid a 'bare corner' appearance.
Bathroom scenes must include styled surfaces and accessories to avoid a bare, empty appearance.
Bedroom renders must show the full furniture set and styling layers to avoid a bare, unfinished appearance.
Bedroom scenes must include layered, cozy styling (throws, cushions, rugs) to avoid a flat, bare appearance.

When a bedroom wall carries two full-height door openings side by side, the reading must not build both as doors: it must check the plan for a window, a built-in closet opening, or a wall line and resolve the second opening accordingly before the model stage.
The exterior site must carry the reference's planting and hardscape (hedges, trees, a path to the entrance) so the facade is not a bare white box.
The entrance must read as a designed threshold: a path and a front court (and seating where the reference shows it) rather than a bare slab door.

The fitting stage must not fall back to a parametric mesh for a wall_cabinet when a library model of the correct type and size exists; it must search the library for a wall_cabinet model that fits the drawn footprint before using parametric.
